limitations: Single-reviewer dossier; not eligible for data/vulnerabilities.jsonl yet.
No XML parser, C harness or PoC was built or executed; the finding is static. The fix commit ships a PoC harness and a compressed input, which were read as text only.
The minimum nesting depth needed to exhaust a stack depends on the platform stack limit and on compiler optimization; no measurement was made.
The call is reached only when the embedding application registers XML_SetElementDeclHandler; parsers that do not register it take the handleDefault path and skip build_model.

The advisory notes the expected impact may include arbitrary code execution in the embedding application; the cataloged category is denial of service because stack exhaustion is what the code defect directly causes.
The OSV fixed event names the 2.4.5 release-preparation merge commit (97a48405), not the code fix 9b4ce651; the advisory, Changes file and tag ancestry were used to confirm the fix.
The MITRE CNA record is a placeholder (vendor/product/version and problemTypes all n/a) and supplies no CVSS or CWE; CWE-674 and the CVSS score come from NVD.

critical_operation.description: build_node converts one scaffold node; when the node is a group it iterates its children and calls build_node recursively for each. The scaffold depth equals the nesting depth in the DTD element content model, which the attacker controls, and no depth limit exists. A deeply nested group therefore consumes one C stack frame per level and can exhaust the stack. The 2.4.5 fix removes build_node and performs the same traversal iteratively using the target XML_Content array as a temporary stack.

entry_point.description: doProlog parses a DTD element declaration. On GROUP_CLOSE, when the application has registered an element declaration handler, it calls build_model at line 5423, which calls build_node with the root scaffold node. The attacker-supplied XML document supplies the nesting that determines recursion depth; applications without XML_SetElementDeclHandler skip the call.
